questions.question: What is synchronization in Java? Why is it needed, and what guarantees does it provide?
questions.title: What Is Synchronization in Java — Mutual Exclusion and Memory Visibility Explained
questions.direct_answer: **Synchronization** is how Java serializes access to shared mutable state so that concurrent code stays correct. It provides **two guarantees**: **mutual exclusion** (only one thread executes the protected section at a time) and **memory visibility** (writes made inside a synchronized block by one thread are visible to any thread that later acquires the same lock). Without synchronization, you get **race conditions** (lost updates) and **visibility bugs** (a thread reads stale values because the CPU cache hasn't flushed). Java provides multiple tools: the **`synchronized` keyword** (intrinsic monitor locks), **`volatile`** (visibility only, no atomicity), **`java.util.concurrent.atomic`** (lock-free atomics), and the **`java.util.concurrent.locks`** package (`ReentrantLock`, `StampedLock`, `ReadWriteLock`). Synchronization is enforced through the **Java Memory Model (JSR 133)** via happens-before relationships.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows BOTH problems synchronization solves (atomicity + visibility), not just 'preventing two threads from running the same code'
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mentioning only mutual exclusion. Missing the visibility / memory-model angle entirely. Confusing `volatile` (visibility only) with `synchronized` (both)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Java Memory Model, happens-before, that uncontended `synchronized` is optimized with biased/lightweight locking, and that modern code prefers `j.u.c.atomic` and `ReentrantLock` over raw `synchronized` for fine control

sections.title: Why Shared Mutable State Is Dangerous — Two Problems, Not One
sections.content:
Concurrent programs are hard because two or more threads share the same heap. The moment you have one mutable field that multiple threads touch, you face **two distinct bugs**:

**1. Race conditions (atomicity)**. A seemingly simple operation like `counter++` is actually **three operations**: read the current value, add one, write the result. If two threads execute this interleaved, one update is lost:
```
Thread A: read 5
Thread B: read 5
Thread A: write 6
Thread B: write 6   // A's increment is lost; counter is 6 instead of 7
```

**2. Memory visibility**. Modern CPUs don't write directly to RAM — they write to per-core caches (L1, L2) and flush them later. Without synchronization, thread B running on another core may **never see** thread A's write. This isn't a hypothetical: real-world examples include infinite loops reading a stale `boolean running` flag, and threads reading a half-constructed object because the JVM reordered writes for performance.

**Synchronization solves both**. When thread A releases a lock and thread B acquires the same lock, the JVM guarantees:
- Mutual exclusion — B couldn't enter while A was inside.
- Visibility — every write A made inside the lock is visible to B.
- Ordering — writes don't get reordered across the lock boundary (no reads from inside can float out).

This is the **happens-before** relationship, formalized in the Java Memory Model (JSR 133, Java 5).

sections.title: The Tools Java Gives You — A Layered Stack
Which Tool Guarantees What
sections.content:
| Tool | Mutual Exclusion | Visibility | Atomicity (composite ops) | Other |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `synchronized` block | Yes | Yes | Yes | Reentrant; uninterruptible |
| `volatile` field | No | Yes | **No** — reads and writes are atomic individually, but `x++` is not | Cheapest memory barrier |
| `AtomicInteger`/`AtomicLong` | No (lock-free) | Yes | Yes for single-variable CAS | Fast uncontended |
| `ReentrantLock` | Yes | Yes | Yes | TryLock, timeout, interruptible, multi-condition |
| `StampedLock` | Optimistic read + write | Yes | Yes | Faster for read-heavy workloads |
| `ReadWriteLock` | Multiple readers OR one writer | Yes | Yes | Great when reads dominate writes |
| `synchronized static method` | Yes (Class monitor) | Yes | Yes | Per-Class, not per-instance |

sections.title: How `synchronized` Works Under the Hood
sections.content:
Every Java object has a hidden **mark word** in its header — the monitor state. HotSpot uses a three-tier locking strategy to keep uncontended synchronization cheap:

1. **Biased locking** (deprecated/removed in Java 15+) — stamped the thread ID on first acquisition; subsequent reentrancies were free for that thread.
2. **Lightweight locking** — uses atomic CAS on the mark word. Very fast in the uncontended case (tens of nanoseconds).
3. **Heavyweight locking** — under contention, inflates to an OS-level monitor (mutex + condition variable). Now blocked threads park via `pthread_cond_wait`, costing microseconds per block-unblock.

**Key properties**:
- **Reentrant** — a thread that holds the lock can enter another `synchronized` block on the same object. Count tracked in the lock structure.
- **Uninterruptible** — a thread waiting to acquire `synchronized` cannot be interrupted. Use `ReentrantLock.lockInterruptibly()` when cancellation matters.
- **Not fair** — doesn't guarantee FIFO acquisition order. Under heavy contention, a thread can be starved.
- **Release on exception** — the JVM implicitly releases the monitor if the block exits via exception, same as a finally block.

sections.title: When to Use Each Synchronization Primitive
sections.content:
**Use `synchronized`** for:
- Simple mutual exclusion where reentrancy and compound operations are needed.
- Legacy code or when you want JVM-managed release on exceptions.
- Narrow critical sections — always prefer `synchronized(someLock) { ... }` block form over `synchronized` on `this`/methods for finer control and to avoid external callers locking your object.

**Use `volatile`** for:
- Simple one-writer-many-readers flags: `volatile boolean running = true`.
- Double-checked locking's `volatile` field (Java 5+) for singleton idioms.
- Never for compound operations like increment.

**Use `java.util.concurrent.atomic`** for:
- Counters, sequence generators, lock-free state machines.
- `LongAdder`/`LongAccumulator` for heavily contended counters — often 10–100× faster than `AtomicLong` under contention.

**Use `ReentrantLock`** for:
- When you need `tryLock(timeout)` to avoid indefinite waits.
- Fairness requirements (`new ReentrantLock(true)` — FIFO, slower but prevents starvation).
- Interruptible acquisition during shutdown paths.
- Multiple condition variables on one lock.

**Use `StampedLock` or `ReadWriteLock`** for:
- Read-heavy, write-rare workloads (config caches, routing tables).
- `StampedLock` is usually faster and newer, but non-reentrant.

**Prefer concurrent collections** over hand-synchronized wrappers:
- `ConcurrentHashMap` instead of `Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>())`.
- `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for read-heavy listener lists.
- `BlockingQueue` family for producer-consumer pipelines.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Synchronization provides **mutual exclusion**, **memory visibility**, and **ordering** — all three, not just the first.
- Without it, you get **race conditions** (lost updates) and **visibility bugs** (stale cached reads).
- **`synchronized`** guarantees all three; **`volatile`** guarantees visibility only; **`AtomicXxx`** provides single-variable atomicity.
- Every Java object has a **monitor**; `synchronized` acquires/releases it with reentrancy tracking.
- Uncontended `synchronized` is fast (tens of ns); under contention it inflates to OS-level mutex.
- Prefer **`ReentrantLock`** for tryLock, fairness, interruptibility, or multiple conditions.
- Prefer **`ConcurrentHashMap`**, **`BlockingQueue`**, and **atomic classes** over hand-synchronized code.
- Synchronization is formalized by the **Java Memory Model (JSR 133)** via **happens-before** relationships.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Synchronization is how Java serializes access to shared mutable state.

**Why it's needed — two separate problems**
- **Race conditions** — `counter++` is actually read-add-write; two threads interleaving lose updates
- **Memory visibility** — CPUs write to per-core caches; one thread may never see another thread's write without synchronization
- Classic symptom: a `while(running)` loop never exits because the other thread's `running = false` is cached

**The three guarantees `synchronized` provides**
- **Mutual exclusion** — only one thread inside the protected section
- **Memory visibility** — writes inside the block are visible after another thread acquires the same lock
- **Ordering** — no reordering of reads or writes across the lock boundary
- These are formalized by the **Java Memory Model (JSR 133)** via **happens-before** relationships

**The tool layers in Java**
- **`synchronized`** — all three guarantees; simplest; reentrant; uninterruptible
- **`volatile`** — visibility only, NOT atomicity; perfect for one-writer-many-readers flags
- **`java.util.concurrent.atomic`** — lock-free atomics: `AtomicInteger`, `AtomicReference`, `LongAdder`
- **`ReentrantLock`** — `synchronized` on steroids: `tryLock(timeout)`, fairness, interruptibility, multiple conditions
- **`StampedLock`** / **`ReadWriteLock`** — for read-heavy workloads
- **Concurrent collections** — `ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, `BlockingQueue`

**How `synchronized` works internally**
- Every Java object has a hidden mark word for monitor state
- Uncontended: lightweight lock with CAS on the mark word — tens of nanoseconds
- Under contention: inflates to an OS mutex; blocked threads park in the kernel
- Reentrant: a thread that owns the lock can enter again
- Automatically released on exception (implicit finally)

**Common pitfalls**
- `volatile` on a counter — doesn't make `counter++` atomic
- Synchronizing on `this` or on public fields — external code can also synchronize on them, causing unexpected contention; always use a **private final lock object**
- Large `synchronized` blocks — hold the lock longer than needed, reducing throughput
- Nested locks in inconsistent order — deadlock

**Recommendation:** Reach for the **lightest tool that fits**. Flag-style visibility → `volatile`. Simple counters → `AtomicInteger` or `LongAdder`. Small critical sections → `synchronized(privateLock)` with a private final lock object. Need tryLock, fairness, or interruptibility → `ReentrantLock`. Shared maps/queues → concurrent collections from `java.util.concurrent`. Never hand-roll synchronization when a concurrent collection or atomic exists — the JDK implementations are battle-tested and much faster than what you'd build under contention.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`synchronized` does two things: mutual exclusion (one thread at a time) and memory visibility (writes become visible when a thread exits the block).

**Monitor basics:**
- Every Java object has an intrinsic monitor
- Instance methods sync on `this`; static methods sync on the `Class` object
- Synchronized blocks let you choose the monitor explicitly — prefer blocks over method-level sync for finer control

- Use `private final Object lock` instead of `this` — external code can sync on your object, causing unexpected contention
- Never synchronize on String literals — interned strings share a monitor across the entire JVM

- Uncontended synchronization is nearly free — the JVM uses lightweight CAS-based locking (biased/lightweight locking)
- Cost becomes significant only under contention when multiple threads compete for the same monitor

I recommend `synchronized` for simple critical sections and `ReentrantLock` when you need `tryLock()`, interruptible acquisition, or multiple conditions.

questions.question: What's the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block in Java? When should you use each?
questions.title: Synchronized Method vs Synchronized Block in Java — Granularity and Lock Object Tradeoffs
questions.direct_answer: Both acquire Java's intrinsic monitor, but they differ in **scope and lock object**. A **synchronized method** locks the entire method body on `this` (instance method) or `Class<?>` (static method). A **synchronized block** lets you wrap a **smaller subset of code** and **choose the lock object explicitly** — usually a `private final Object lock = new Object();`. **Prefer synchronized blocks** in modern code for three reasons: **smaller critical sections** (higher throughput under contention), **private lock objects** (external callers can't accidentally synchronize on your public instance and deadlock you), and **multiple locks per class** (different fields guarded by different monitors). Synchronized methods are acceptable only for small classes with a single invariant where the whole method IS the critical section.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows that synchronized method locks on `this` (or Class for static), understands why that's a problem (external code can acquire it), and prefers block form with private lock object
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that `synchronized` on a method locks on `this` — assuming it creates an invisible private lock. Synchronizing on `String` literals, `Boolean.TRUE`, or other interned/shared objects
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that `synchronized` on `this` exposes your lock to external code (any caller can `synchronized(yourObj) {...}` and block your methods), and that separate fields should be guarded by separate lock objects to allow independent access

sections.title: Same Mechanism, Different Granularity and Lock Object
Synchronized Method vs Block
sections.content:
| Aspect | Synchronized Method | Synchronized Block |
|---|---|---|
| **Lock object** | `this` (instance) or `Class<?>` (static) — implicit | **Explicit** — you choose |
| **Scope** | Entire method body | Exactly the statements you wrap |
| **Lock visibility to callers** | Public — anyone can `synchronized(yourObj)` too | Private — lock is encapsulated |
| **Lock hold time** | Often longer than necessary | Minimized |
| **Multiple independent locks per class** | Difficult (only `this` or Class) | Trivial — one private lock per field group |
| **Bytecode** | Implicit `monitorenter` on method entry | Explicit `monitorenter`/`monitorexit` |
| **Preferred for** | Small classes, whole-method invariant | Everything else (the default choice) |

sections.title: Why Locking on `this` Is a Quiet Trap
Static Synchronized — Watch Out for the Class Monitor
What Never to Lock On
sections.content:
Certain objects look like reasonable locks but are in fact shared across the entire JVM, causing mysterious contention or deadlock:

**String literals and interned Strings**:
```java
synchronized ("lock") { ... } // BUG
```
Every piece of code in the JVM that uses the same literal shares the same interned String and thus the same monitor.

**Boxed primitives (`Integer`, `Long`, `Boolean`)**:
```java
synchronized (someInteger) { ... } // BUG
```
Autoboxing caches small `Integer` values (-128..127). `Boolean.TRUE`/`FALSE` are singletons. Unrelated classes can accidentally share the monitor.

**Mutable fields**:
```java
synchronized (this.data) { ... } // BUG if data can be reassigned
```
If `data` is reassigned while you hold the lock, a later acquirer of `synchronized(this.data)` gets a different monitor — no mutual exclusion.

**Lock objects held by third-party code**.

**The right pattern**: always use a `private final Object lock = new Object();` field. It's guaranteed unique, unshared, and immutable.

sections.title: When Each Form Is Appropriate
sections.content:
**Synchronized method is acceptable when**:
- The class is small with a single invariant (e.g., a counter, a bounded stack).
- Every method genuinely needs to serialize on the same lock.
- The method body IS the critical section with no logging/I/O to exclude.
- You accept that external code can acquire your lock.

**Synchronized block is preferred when** (the 95% case):
- The critical section is smaller than the full method.
- You want a private lock object for encapsulation and safety.
- Different fields need independent locks (fine-grained locking).
- You might later switch to `ReentrantLock` — the block form already localizes the lock variable.

**Go beyond `synchronized` entirely when**:
- You need `tryLock(timeout)`, interruptibility, or fairness → `ReentrantLock`.
- Read-heavy workload → `ReadWriteLock` or `StampedLock`.
- Single-variable atomicity → `AtomicInteger`/`LongAdder`.
- Shared map/queue/list → `ConcurrentHashMap`, `BlockingQueue`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`.

**Always**:
- Use private final lock objects.
- Keep critical sections short — no I/O, no network calls, no user callbacks inside a lock.
- Document the invariant a lock protects with a comment or `@GuardedBy` annotation (from Error Prone / FindBugs).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Both forms use the same JVM intrinsic monitor mechanism; difference is **lock object and scope**.
- **Synchronized method** locks on `this` (instance) or `Class<?>` (static) — a **public** lock.
- **Synchronized block** lets you use a **private final lock object** — safer and more granular.
- **External callers can acquire `this` or `Class`** — that's why private lock objects matter.
- **Instance and static synchronized methods use different monitors** — they don't exclude each other.
- **Never synchronize on String literals, boxed primitives, or mutable fields** — shared/unstable monitors.
- Keep critical sections **small** — no I/O, logging, or user callbacks inside.
- **Prefer block form** as the default; use method form only for small, whole-method invariants.
- For complex coordination, graduate to `ReentrantLock`, `StampedLock`, or `java.util.concurrent.atomic`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Both synchronized methods and blocks use Java's intrinsic monitor. The difference is **what you lock on** and **how much code is inside the critical section**.

**Synchronized method**
- The entire method body is locked
- Instance method locks on **`this`**
- Static method locks on **`Class<?>`**
- Convenient but coarse-grained

**Synchronized block**
- You wrap only the statements that need protection
- You choose the lock object explicitly
- Typically a **`private final Object lock = new Object()`**

**Why I prefer the block form in production**

**Problem 1: Locking on `this` exposes your lock to external code**
- Any caller with a reference to your object can write `synchronized(yourObj) { Thread.sleep(60_000); }` and freeze every `synchronized` method on it
- Frameworks, logging wrappers, test code — any of them can accidentally do this
- A private lock field is encapsulated and unreachable from outside

**Problem 2: Coarse-grained locking**
- If a class has ten synchronized methods, all ten serialize on `this`
- A read of field A blocks a write to unrelated field B
- With separate private lock objects per field group, they don't contend

**Problem 3: Lock held during I/O**
- `public synchronized void transfer()` holds the lock for the entire method including slow logging, audit, and network calls
- With a block, I shrink the critical section to just the balance update — throughput under contention goes up dramatically

**Watch out for `static synchronized`**
- Locks on `MyClass.class`, not `this`
- Does NOT block instance-synchronized methods of the same class — they use different monitors
- The `Class` object is globally accessible; same external-lock problem
- Prefer `private static final Object CLASS_LOCK = new Object()`

**Things you must never lock on**
- String literals — interned, shared JVM-wide
- Boxed primitives like `Integer.valueOf(1)` — cached singletons
- `Boolean.TRUE`/`FALSE` — singletons
- Mutable fields — reassignment breaks exclusion

**The right idiom every time**
```java
private final Object lock = new Object();
public void foo() {
    synchronized (lock) { /* smallest critical section */ }
}
```

**Recommendation:** Default to `synchronized` **blocks** with **private final lock objects**. Use synchronized methods only when the class is small with one invariant and the whole method truly IS the critical section. Never lock on `this`, `Class`, String literals, or boxed primitives. Mark guarded fields with `@GuardedBy("lock")` (from Error Prone) for documentation and static analysis. And for anything beyond simple mutual exclusion, look at `ReentrantLock` (tryLock, fairness, interruptibility) or the lock-free tools in `java.util.concurrent.atomic`.

Synchronized block is preferred when (the 95% case): The critical section is smaller than the full method. You want a private lock object for encapsulation and safety. Different fields need independent locks (fine-grained locking). You might later switch to ReentrantLock.

Both synchronized methods and synchronized blocks acquire the same intrinsic monitor mechanism in the JVM. The JVM treats them equivalently under the hood — the compiler translates them to the same monitorenter/monitorexit bytecodes. The difference is entirely about what you lock on and how much code is inside the critical section. Synchronized method — the entire method body is the.

questions.question: What are the differences between the synchronized keyword and ReentrantLock, and when should you choose each?
questions.direct_answer: synchronized is the simpler, JVM-managed lock that automatically releases on scope exit and benefits from JIT optimisations like biased locking. ReentrantLock provides explicit control: interruptible acquisition, timed tryLock, multiple Condition variables, and fairness policies. Choose ReentrantLock when you need any of those advanced features; otherwise prefer synchronized for its clarity and safety.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's two locking models and the practical tradeoffs between simplicity and control.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to call lock.unlock() in a finally block with ReentrantLock, causing a permanent lock if an exception is thrown.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`synchronized` = simpler, automatic unlock; `ReentrantLock` = three extra capabilities**.
- **`tryLock(timeout)`** — returns false after timeout instead of blocking indefinitely; prevents permanent waits.
- **`lockInterruptibly()`** — throws `InterruptedException` for responsive shutdown; BLOCKED on `synchronized` cannot be interrupted.
- **Multiple `Condition` objects** — producers await `notFull`, consumers await `notEmpty`; precise wakeups vs single `wait` queue.
- **Forgetting `unlock()` in `finally` = permanent deadlock** — never forget the `try { ... } finally { lock.unlock(); }` pattern.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`synchronized` is simpler — the JVM manages lock/unlock automatically. `ReentrantLock` adds three capabilities that `synchronized` lacks.

**Three reasons to use ReentrantLock:**
- `tryLock(timeout)`: returns false after timeout instead of blocking indefinitely — prevents permanent waits
- `lockInterruptibly()`: throws `InterruptedException` for responsive shutdown; a thread BLOCKED on `synchronized` cannot be interrupted
- Multiple `Condition` objects: producers `await` on `notFull`, consumers on `notEmpty` — separate wait queues, precise wakeups

**What synchronized still has:**
- Automatic unlock — forgetting `unlock()` in a `finally` block with ReentrantLock is a permanent deadlock
- Slightly more concise syntax for simple cases
- JVM can apply lock elision and bias optimization transparently

**Both are reentrant:**
- A thread holding the lock can re-acquire it without deadlocking
- ReentrantLock also offers a fairness option for FIFO ordering — avoid it for performance unless starvation is observed

I recommend `synchronized` for simple critical sections and `ReentrantLock` only when you need timeout, interruptibility, or multiple conditions.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
**Synchronization** is how Java serializes access to shared mutable state so that concurrent code stays correct.

It provides **two guarantees**: **mutual exclusion** (only one thread executes the protected section at a time) and **memory visibility** (writes made inside a synchronized block by one thread are visible to any thread that later acquires the same lock).

synchronized is the simpler, JVM-managed lock that automatically releases on scope exit and benefits from JIT optimisations like biased locking. ReentrantLock provides explicit control: interruptible acquisition, timed tryLock, multiple Condition variables, and fairness policies. Choose ReentrantLock when you need any of those advanced features; otherwise prefer synchronized for its clarity and safety.

Mentioning only mutual exclusion. Missing the visibility / memory-model angle entirely. Confusing `volatile` (visibility only) with `synchronized` (both)

sections.title: Capabilities, Safety, and When Each Is the Right Choice
sections.content:
The table shows that ReentrantLock adds flexibility at the cost of manual management.

| Feature | synchronized | ReentrantLock |
|---|---|---|
| Lock acquisition | Automatic (enter block/method) | Manual — `lock()` |
| Lock release | Automatic (exit block/method) | Manual — `unlock()` in `finally` |
| Timeout | No — blocks indefinitely | Yes — `tryLock(timeout, unit)` |
| Interruptible waiting | No | Yes — `lockInterruptibly()` |
| Multiple conditions | No — one wait set per monitor | Yes — `newCondition()` creates separate wait queues |
| Fairness option | No (always unfair) | Yes — `new ReentrantLock(true)` for FIFO ordering |
| Reentrant | Yes | Yes |
| Deadlock risk from forgetting unlock | None | High — must use `finally` |

The **fairness** row is a hidden cost. Fair locks guarantee FIFO ordering but add overhead — each acquisition checks the wait queue. Unfair locks (the default for both) allow barging, where a newly arriving thread can acquire the lock ahead of waiting threads. This is usually desirable because it reduces context switches.

sections.title: How the choices differ
sections.content: Both acquire Java's intrinsic monitor, but they differ in **scope and lock object**. A **synchronized method** locks the entire method body on `this` (instance method) or `Class<?>` (static method). A **synchronized block** lets you wrap a **smaller subset of code** and **choose the lock object explicitly** — usually a `private final Object lock = new Object();`. **Prefer synchronized blocks** in modern code for three reasons: **smaller critical sections** (higher throughput under contention), **private lock objects** (external callers can't accidentally synchronize on your public instance and deadlock you), and **multiple locks per class** (different fields guarded by different monitors). Synchronized methods are acceptable only for small classes with a single invariant where the whole method IS the critical section.

questions.title: ReentrantReadWriteLock — Use Cases and Pitfalls
questions.question: How does ReentrantReadWriteLock work, when should you use it over a plain ReentrantLock, and what are its main pitfalls?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of read-write lock semantics and the ability to identify scenarios where it genuinely helps versus adds complexity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using ReentrantReadWriteLock when writes are as frequent as reads — the overhead of managing two lock states makes it slower than a simple ReentrantLock in write-heavy workloads.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss write-lock starvation (readers can starve writers in a fair=false configuration), lock downgrade (write->read), and that lock upgrade (read->write) is NOT supported.

questions.direct_answer: ReentrantReadWriteLock allows multiple concurrent readers OR one exclusive writer. It improves throughput for read-heavy workloads. Main pitfalls: write-lock starvation under non-fair mode, no lock upgrade (read->write), and overhead that makes it slower than a plain lock for write-heavy or low-contention workloads.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Shared read lock + exclusive write lock** — multiple readers proceed simultaneously; a writer needs everyone out.
- **Read lock CANNOT be upgraded to write lock** — thread deadlocks waiting for itself to release the read lock.
- **Write lock CAN be downgraded to read lock** — acquire write, acquire read, release write; other readers join.
- **Writer starvation** — continuous readers can indefinitely block a waiting writer; fair mode (FIFO) prevents this at cost of throughput.
- **Not always faster than a simple lock** — overhead of shared-lock management exceeds benefit when reads take nanoseconds.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
ReentrantReadWriteLock separates access into a shared read lock and an exclusive write lock — multiple readers proceed simultaneously, but a writer needs everyone out.

**How it works:**
- Read lock: shared — any number of threads can hold it simultaneously; no write can proceed while readers hold it
- Write lock: exclusive — no reader or writer can proceed while held

**Upgrade/downgrade rules:**
- Read lock CANNOT be upgraded to write lock — thread deadlocks waiting for itself to release the read lock
- Write lock CAN be downgraded to read lock — acquire write, then acquire read, then release write; other readers can now join

**Writer starvation:**
- Continuous readers can indefinitely block a waiting writer
- Fair mode (`true` in constructor) prevents this with FIFO ordering, at the cost of lower throughput

**Not always faster:**
- If reads are trivially fast (nanoseconds), shared-lock management overhead exceeds the concurrency benefit
- Pays off when reads take milliseconds and vastly outnumber writes

I recommend ReadWriteLock for read-heavy caches and configuration stores. For very high read contention, consider StampedLock's optimistic read mode.

sections.content:
- **Optimistic read: read without locking, then validate** — if validation succeeds, no write occurred and data is consistent.

- **`tryConvertToWriteLock()` can upgrade read to write** — impossible with ReentrantReadWriteLock (would deadlock).

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
StampedLock adds optimistic reading — you read without acquiring any lock, then validate whether a write happened during the read.

**Optimistic read pattern:**
- `tryOptimisticRead()` returns a stamp without locking — read the data, then `validate(stamp)`
- Validation succeeds: no write occurred, data is consistent — proceed
- Validation fails: fall back to a pessimistic read lock or retry
- Near-free when writes are rare — avoids CAS and shared-lock tracking entirely

**Critical requirement:**
- Must validate the stamp after every optimistic read — forgetting creates a silent data race that works most of the time but corrupts under write contention

**Limitations:**
- Not reentrant — re-acquiring the write lock from the same thread deadlocks
- Does not implement the `Lock` interface — no `Condition` support

**Advantage over ReadWriteLock:**
- `tryConvertToWriteLock()` can upgrade a read to a write lock without deadlocking — impossible with ReentrantReadWriteLock

I recommend StampedLock for geometry-style data (coordinates, spatial data) with very frequent reads and rare writes. ReentrantReadWriteLock is safer and simpler for most other scenarios.

questions.title: wait/notify vs Condition.await/signal
questions.question: Compare Object.wait()/notify() with Condition.await()/signal() from java.util.concurrent.locks. When would you choose one over the other?

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the evolution from intrinsic locks to explicit locks, and the practical benefits of Condition over wait/notify.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting that wait() must always be called in a loop to guard against spurious wakeups, and that the same is true for Condition.await().
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Point out that a single Lock can have multiple Condition objects, enabling selective notification — impossible with intrinsic wait/notify which share one condition queue per object.

questions.direct_answer: Both implement the monitor pattern for thread cooperation, but Condition is strictly more powerful. It supports multiple condition queues per lock, timed waits with interruption control, and integrates cleanly with ReentrantLock. Prefer Condition for new code that needs explicit locking.

sections.title: notify() Wakes a Random Waiting Thread — Condition.signal() Wakes Exactly the Right One
sections.content:
The fundamental problem with `Object.wait()/notify()` is **imprecision**. All threads waiting on a monitor share a single wait set. When you call `notify()`, the JVM wakes **one arbitrary thread** — it might be the producer when you meant to wake a consumer, or vice versa. `notifyAll()` wakes all threads, but most re-check their condition, find it unsatisfied, and go back to sleep — wasting CPU cycles.

`Condition` objects from `ReentrantLock.newCondition()` solve this by creating **separate wait queues**. A producer waiting for space uses `notFull.await()`. A consumer waiting for items uses `notEmpty.await()`. When an item is added, you call `notEmpty.signal()` — only a consumer wakes up. When an item is removed, you call `notFull.signal()` — only a producer wakes up.

Both mechanisms require the thread to hold the lock when calling `wait()/await()` and both release the lock atomically while waiting. Both are subject to **spurious wakeups** — the thread can wake without being signaled. This is why waiting must always be in a **while loop**, never an `if` statement.

The wait loop pattern is identical for both: `while (!condition) { obj.wait(); }` or `while (!condition) { cond.await(); }`. The loop re-checks the condition after every wakeup, handling spurious wakes and race conditions from `notifyAll()`.

sections.title: Precision, Flexibility, and API Differences: wait/notify vs Condition
sections.content:
The table shows that Condition provides **targeted signaling** while wait/notify uses a single shared wait set.

| Feature | Object.wait()/notify() | Condition.await()/signal() |
|---|---|---|
| Lock mechanism | synchronized monitor | ReentrantLock |
| Wait sets | One per monitor | Multiple — newCondition() creates separate queues |
| Wake precision | notify() wakes one random thread | signal() wakes one thread from this specific Condition |
| Wake all | notifyAll() wakes all waiters | signalAll() wakes all on this Condition only |
| Timed wait | wait(millis) — returns void | await(timeout, unit) — returns false on timeout |
| Interruptible | Always (throws InterruptedException) | Both interruptible and uninterruptible (awaitUninterruptibly) |
| Must hold lock | Yes — synchronized block required | Yes — lock.lock() required |

The **wait sets** row is the architectural difference. With wait/notify, producers and consumers share one queue — notify() might wake a producer when a consumer should wake. With Condition, each role has its own queue and is signaled independently.

sections.title: Why wait() Must Always Be in a While Loop — The Spurious Wakeup Problem
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`wait()`/`notify()` uses one shared wait queue** — `notify()` wakes an arbitrary thread; might wake wrong type.
- **`Condition` objects from ReentrantLock create separate queues** — producers await `notFull`, consumers await `notEmpty`.
- **`signal()` wakes exactly one from the right queue** — no wasted context switches; more precise than `notifyAll()`.
- **Always use `while (!condition) await()`** — spurious wakeups are real; `if` instead of `while` is a correctness bug.
- **`await(timeout)` returns false on timeout** — `Object.wait(millis)` returns void; cannot distinguish timeout from notify.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`wait()`/`notify()` uses one shared wait queue for all waiters — `Condition` objects create separate queues, making wakeups precise.

**Problem with wait/notify:**
- `notify()` wakes an arbitrary thread — might wake a producer when you need a consumer
- `notifyAll()` wakes everyone but most immediately go back to sleep — wasted context switches

**Condition objects:**
- Created from ReentrantLock: `Condition notFull = lock.newCondition()`
- Producers `await` on `notFull`, consumers on `notEmpty` — `signal()` wakes exactly one from the correct queue

**The while loop pattern (mandatory):**
- `while (!condition) await()` — spurious wakeups are real; using `if` instead of `while` causes correctness bugs
- `Condition.await()` supports timed waiting that returns `false` on timeout — `Object.wait(millis)` returns void and can't distinguish timeout from notification

I recommend Condition objects with ReentrantLock for all producer-consumer patterns. `wait()`/`notify()` with synchronized is functional but less precise and harder to reason about correctly.

beats.text: The fundamental problem with Object.wait()/notify() is imprecision. All threads waiting on a monitor share a single wait set. When you call notify(), the JVM wakes one arbitrary thread — it might be the producer when you meant to wake a consumer, or vice versa. notifyAll() wakes all threads, but most re-check their condition, find it unsatisfied, and go back to sleep — wasting CPU cycles. Condition objects from ReentrantLock.newCondition() solve this by creating separate wait queues. A producer waiting for space uses notFull.await(). A consumer waiting for items uses notEmpty.await().

questions.title: AtomicInteger vs synchronized — When to Use Each
questions.question: When should you use AtomicInteger (and other Atomic classes) versus synchronized for thread-safe counters and shared state?
questions.direct_answer: AtomicInteger uses hardware-level compare-and-swap (CAS) to perform single-variable updates without a lock, making it faster under low-to-medium contention for single-variable operations. synchronized (or explicit locks) are necessary for multi-variable invariants or compound operations that span several fields. For high-contention counters, LongAdder can outperform both by maintaining per-CPU cells.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of lock-free programming fundamentals and when CAS-based classes provide a real performance benefit.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming AtomicInteger is always faster — under very high contention, CAS spin-retry can waste more CPU than a fair lock, and LongAdder is the better choice for pure incrementing.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention ABA problem in CAS, the existence of AtomicStampedReference to mitigate it, and LongAdder as the contention-optimised counter.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`AtomicInteger` uses CAS** — CPU-level Compare-And-Swap; atomically reads, compares, writes; no lock acquired.
- **Under high contention, CAS spinning burns CPU** — cache-line bouncing between cores; `synchronized` can outperform.
- **`LongAdder` distributes across cells** — each thread writes to its own cell; `sum()` aggregates; not an atomic snapshot.
- **CAS works on one variable only** — to update two related fields atomically, use `synchronized` or `ReentrantLock`.
- **`LongAdder` for high-contention counters; `AtomicInteger` for moderate contention**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`AtomicInteger` uses CAS — a CPU instruction that atomically reads, compares, and writes without acquiring a lock.

**CAS mechanics:**
- Atomically reads current value, checks if it equals expected, writes new value only if it matches — else retries in a spin loop
- Under low contention: nanoseconds, much faster than acquiring a monitor lock
- Under high contention: spin loop burns CPU; cache-line bouncing between cores makes it worse — synchronized can outperform

**LongAdder (Java 8):**
- Distributes increments across an array of cells — each thread writes to its own cell, avoiding cache-line bouncing
- `sum()` aggregates but is not an atomic snapshot — correct for statistics, not for exact coordination
- Better than `AtomicLong` under high contention scenarios

**CAS limitation:**
- Works on one variable at a time — to update two related fields atomically, use `synchronized` or `ReentrantLock`

I recommend `AtomicInteger` for single-variable counters under moderate contention, `LongAdder` for high-contention statistics counters, and `synchronized` when multiple variables must change together.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
**Synchronization** is how Java serializes access to shared mutable state so that concurrent code stays correct.

It provides **two guarantees**: **mutual exclusion** (only one thread executes the protected section at a time) and **memory visibility** (writes made inside a synchronized block by one thread are visible to any thread that later acquires the same lock).

AtomicInteger uses hardware-level compare-and-swap (CAS) to perform single-variable updates without a lock, making it faster under low-to-medium contention for single-variable operations. synchronized (or explicit locks) are necessary for multi-variable invariants or compound operations that span several fields. For high-contention counters, LongAdder can outperform both by maintaining per-CPU cells.

Mentioning only mutual exclusion. Missing the visibility / memory-model angle entirely. Confusing `volatile` (visibility only) with `synchronized` (both)

sections.title: CAS Internals and When to Choose AtomicInteger vs synchronized vs LongAdder
How the choices differ
sections.content: Both acquire Java's intrinsic monitor, but they differ in **scope and lock object**. A **synchronized method** locks the entire method body on `this` (instance method) or `Class<?>` (static method). A **synchronized block** lets you wrap a **smaller subset of code** and **choose the lock object explicitly** — usually a `private final Object lock = new Object();`. **Prefer synchronized blocks** in modern code for three reasons: **smaller critical sections** (higher throughput under contention), **private lock objects** (external callers can't accidentally synchronize on your public instance and deadlock you), and **multiple locks per class** (different fields guarded by different monitors). Synchronized methods are acceptable only for small classes with a single invariant where the whole method IS the critical section.
